    parts.append(f'\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n{t}\\n')
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(parts))
print(''.join(parts)[:36000])

print('Uniform Q=0.8 accepted as plausible:',0.8 <= 1.5*0.8)

strengths: The paper addresses a practical stitching failure: changing the seam alone cannot repair substantial local misalignment. Figures 1, 10, and 11 show useful improvements in curb, paving, and stair continuity.

Experiments cover 79 image pairs across three datasets, including two public datasets. Comparisons using a common initial alignment, runtime measurements, and a 20-participant preference study provide encouraging evidence for the proposed repair strategy.

The modular pipeline is understandable, and boundary-label constraints provide a sensible mechanism for reconnecting local seams. Established components and public datasets are attributed. Section 4.4 and Figure 12 candidly identify meaningful failure conditions.
weaknesses: The incremental contribution is insufficiently isolated. SSIM-based seam evaluation is inherited from [17], seam-guided alignment is established in [18], and dense correspondence uses SIFT flow [20]. Figure 4 provides a useful qualitative illustration, but systematic ablations do not establish the contribution of the patch-selection rule, sigmoid modification, or local repair relative to simpler alternatives.

The comparative evaluation is narrow relative to the superiority claims. Full-dataset quantitative comparisons cover only seam-cutting methods [16] and [17]; comparisons with alignment-changing methods [18] and [26] are qualitative and limited. Relevant cited alternatives, including warping-residual stitching [12] and the composition network [5], are not evaluated. Testing only alignment method [15] also leaves the claimed broad compatibility empirically unverified.

The sole quantitative quality measure, average seam SSIM in Eq. (5), closely follows the signal used to select repairs and does not assess distortion or artifacts away from the seam. The manuscript itself reports disagreement between this metric and perceived quality. The preference study helps, but its eight manually selected 'controversial' examples do not establish representative performance, and uncertainty is not reported. Table 1 also contains a minor reporting inconsistency: the baseline rows total 159 and 161 rankings instead of 160 each.

The claim that the method can 'almost remove' the rough-alignment assumption exceeds the demonstrated scope. Section 3.4 assumes pre-aligned patches with little residual parallax, and Section 4.4 requires errors to be localized. Moreover, the acceptance rule max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) accepts uniformly high-error seams, so it detects relative error peaks rather than establishing acceptable quality. These restrictions warrant narrower claims and robustness evaluation.

The central warp needs a more precise specification for reproducibility. Equation (4) defines a scalar sigmoid of spatial position, while the algorithm describes applying f directly to a vector flow; the exact weighting operation, orientation handling, and treatment of overlapping repair patches remain unclear. Fixed boundary labels ensure label compatibility but do not establish the assertion that subsequent alignment cannot worsen results.
